overview.intro:
Chapter 21 is the "everything else" chapter of the food schedule: coffee and tea extracts, yeasts, sauces and seasonings, soups, ice cream and — in heading 2106 — dietary supplements, protein concentrates, drink mixes and flavored syrups. Its **118 tariff lines** run from Free on instant coffee to $1.996/kg on over-quota butter substitutes, and half the trade sits under one subheading: **2106.90**, mostly 2106.90.99 at 6.4%.

The U.S. imported **$12.14B** of these goods in 2025. **Singapore** ($2.18B, almost all food preparations) and **Canada** ($2.04B) were the largest suppliers, then Mexico and Italy. On top of the base rate comes an **extra duty by country**: since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff on 60 economies — +12.5% for Singapore (12.5% in all when the U.S.–Singapore FTA makes the base rate Free), 10% in total for the EU, +20% for China (+37.5% on soy sauce and protein concentrates) and +37.5% for Brazil. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (except Canadian sugar and dairy goods entered above Canada's USMCA quotas, which pay the over-quota rate plus 10%), and six coffee, tea, sugar-syrup and fortified orange juice lines are exempt for every country. Lines that contain sugar or dairy are also under **tariff-rate quotas**: a low rate inside the quota, a high per-kilogram rate above it.

productGroups.label: Coffee, tea & maté extracts and preparations; chicory
productGroups.blurb: Instant coffee and extracts of coffee and tea are Free. Coffee or tea preparations with sugar or dairy fall into quota lines: 10% inside the quota, 30.5¢/kg + 8.5% above it. Other coffee preparations pay 8.5%, roasted chicory 2.1¢/kg.

productGroups.label: Yeasts, dead single-cell micro-organisms & baking powder
productGroups.blurb: Active yeast and most inactive yeast pay 6.4%, other dead micro-organisms 3.2%. Crude dried brewers' yeast and prepared baking powder are Free.

productGroups.label: Sauces, condiments, seasonings & mustard
productGroups.blurb: Soy sauce is 3%, ketchup 6%, other tomato sauces 11.6% and prepared mustard 2.8¢/kg; fish sauce and mustard flour are Free. Mayonnaise, salad dressings, pasta sauces and most seasonings are 6.4%. Seasonings with over 10% cane or beet sugar have a 689-tonne quota: 7.5% inside it, 30.5¢/kg + 6.4% above it.

productGroups.label: Soups, broths & homogenized composite food (baby food)
productGroups.blurb: Soups and broths pay 3.2%. Homogenized composite food (baby food in containers of 250 g or less) pays 2.5% for infants and 6.4% for young children.

productGroups.label: Ice cream & other edible ice
productGroups.blurb: Ice cream is a dairy quota product: 20% for the 5.67 million liters a year allowed in the quota, 50.2¢/kg + 17% above it. Edible ice with no dairy limit — sorbet, ice pops — pays 17%.

productGroups.label: Food preparations n.e.s.i. (supplements, syrups, mixes)
productGroups.blurb: The catch-all heading: dietary supplements, protein concentrates, drink mixes, flavored syrups, non-dairy creamers, herbal tea blends and fortified juice concentrates. Most of it is 2106.90.99 at 6.4%. Lines with dairy or sugar have quotas with over-quota rates up to $1.996/kg, and fortified juice concentrates (2106.90.52, 2106.90.54) pay the rate of the same juice in heading 2009.

workedExamples.body: The general rate is 6.4%. For EU goods whose base rate is under 10%, the 2026 Section 301 action charges 10% in total in place of the base rate (9903.05.39). A $100,000 shipment pays **$10,000** instead of $6,400. FDA rules still apply at entry: the importer needs a foreign supplier verification program (21 CFR 1.511 for supplements), and prior notice must be filed before arrival.

workedExamples.title: Soy sauce from China
workedExamples.body: Soy sauce has a 3% base rate. China pays two Section 301 duties on it: +12.5% under the 2026 action (9903.05.31) and +25% because soy sauce is on List 3 (9903.88.03). That is **40.5%** in total: $20,250 on a $50,000 container. Soy sauce from Japan, by contrast, is Free under the U.S.–Japan Trade Agreement (JP), but the 12.5% Japan total (9903.05.49) still applies.

workedExamples.title: Instant coffee from Brazil
workedExamples.body: Instant coffee is Free, and 2101.11.21 is on both exemption lists: the Brazil Section 301 list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03) and the general 2026 list (note 52(b), 9903.05.86). So Brazil's 37.5% does not apply and the total is **Free**. A coffee *preparation* with sugar (2101.12.58) from Brazil is different: 30.5¢/kg + 8.5% over quota, plus 37.5%.

seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 21 (coffee extracts, sauces, soups, ice cream, food supplements) since January 2025: base rates on all 118 lines, the end of the IEEPA and Section 122 duties, and the 2026 Section 301 tariffs, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). No Chapter 21 base rate changed: 112 of the 118 lines are the same, and the other 6 are new statistical splits (organic soups, and frozen, sugar-containing and organic food preparations under 2106.90.99) that carry their parent line's rate.

Everything that changed came on top of the base rate, as extra duties set by country. The 2025 IEEPA duties (Canada +35%, Mexico +25%, the reciprocal tariff on everyone else) **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026**, goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%**. Six Chapter 21 subheadings are on its general exemption list — instant coffee, coffee and tea extracts, coffee preparations without sugar or dairy, in-quota sugar syrups and fortified orange juice. China pays more because older Section 301 duties stack on top (7.5%, or 25% on soy sauce, other sauces and protein concentrates), and Brazil adds a separate 25%. **USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are still exempt.**
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 21 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the older China Section 301 lists, the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended, and the Canada Section 338 actions (which list no Chapter 21 line). For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

inEffect.exemption: Base rate + 12.5% (9903.05.68). Acai preparations for making beverages (2106.90.99) are exempt by description (note 52(c), 9903.05.87). The U.S.–Singapore FTA (SG) removes the base rate but not the Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)). The IEEPA reciprocal duty ended February 24, 2026.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 21 goods were **$12.14B in 2025**, 4.7% less than the $12.74B of 2024. Half of the total is one product: **food preparations not elsewhere specified (2106.90)**, $6.19B — the subheading that holds dietary supplements, drink preparations, creamers and syrups. Sauces and seasonings (2103.90) come next at $2.03B.

**Singapore** is the largest supplier ($2.18B), and almost all of it is heading 2106. Its shipments fell 19.3% in 2025 and are down from $4.07B in 2022. **China** fell 23.7% to $689M. Going the other way, coffee extracts and instant coffee (2101.11) rose 36% to $1.32B, and **Colombia**, mostly a coffee-extract supplier, grew 54% to $304M. Coffee extracts are Free under the general rate and on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list.

Canada ($2.04B) and Mexico ($1.42B) supplied 29% of 2025 imports; USMCA-qualifying goods from both pay no extra duty. The figures are annual and stop at 2025, before the 2026 tariff changes (the end of the IEEPA duties in February and the Section 301 tariffs from July 24, 2026); they do not show what those changes did. Duty-collected figures are not available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
The total rate on Chapter 21 goods depends as much on **where they come from** as on what they are. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — taken from the current tariff schedule.

Since the IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026, the extra duty is the **Section 301 tariff on 60 economies** that started July 24, 2026. **USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico pay no extra duty**, **EU goods pay 10%** in place of a lower base rate, most other large suppliers add 10% or 12.5%, and **China adds 20% — 37.5% on soy sauce, other sauces and protein concentrates**. Instant coffee, coffee and tea extracts and fortified orange juice are exempt for everyone. On the sugar and dairy quota lines the cell shows the over-quota rate, except where an FTA sets its own quota: there it shows both tiers — Free within Canada's USMCA quotas and the over-quota rate plus 10% above them, or Colombia's rate within its sugar quota and above it.

Quota lines: where a product has an in-quota and an over-quota line, both are in the group; the over-quota rates (for example 30.5¢/kg + 8.5% or 50.2¢/kg + 17%) apply once the quota is filled, and several quotas are set at zero (Chapter 17 additional U.S. notes 7 and 9).

FTA quota lines are priced per tier, the way the calculator asks. USMCA (Canada and Mexico, "USMCA-qualifying" side): goods of Mexico are Free with no limit (9823.xx.01). Goods of Canada are Free within Canada's 2026 USMCA quotas (Chapter 98 subchapter XXIII); above them they pay the over-quota rate printed there plus the 10% Section 301 duty, because U.S. note 52(g) relieves only goods entered free of duty under USMCA — for example "Free within quota / 30.5¢/kg + 18.5% above quota". Colombia: sugar-containing lines are Free within Colombia's TPA sugar quota (9822.08.01) and pay the base rate above it, plus 12.5% either way; the dairy quota lines (9918.04.60–9918.04.80) are Free at any quantity, so they pay 12.5%.

Fortified juice concentrates (2106.90.52, 2106.90.54) have no printed rate: they pay the rate of the same juice in heading 2009. The calculator cannot price them without the matching 2009 line, so their cells stay as text — "Heading 2009 juice rate" plus the country's extra duty — and are not cross-checked.

EU and Japan: the 10% (EU) or 12.5% (Japan) total applies when the base rate, or its ad valorem equivalent, is lower. Per-kilogram base rates are compared at the $10,000 / 1,000 kg test shipment ($10 per kg), so a cheaper product can end up paying only its per-kilogram rate.

Price-based special safeguard duties (Chapter 99 subchapter IV) can add a per-kilogram charge to low-priced over-quota sugar and dairy goods; they do not apply to Canada, Mexico, Singapore, South Korea, Australia and other FTA partners listed there, and are not applied in the matrix.
The IEEPA duties (9903.01.xx, 9903.02.xx) are still printed in the schedule but ended February 24, 2026, and the Section 122 surcharge (9903.03.01) expired July 23, 2026; neither is applied.
industryAreas.exemptionCheck: Read U.S. notes 20, 50, 51 and 52 to Chapter 99 subchapter III in the 2026 Revision 21. The Section 301 general exemption list (note 52(b), 9903.05.86) has six Chapter 21 subheadings: 2101.11.21, 2101.11.29, 2101.12.90, 2101.20.20, 2106.90.44 and 2106.90.48; note 52(c) adds acai preparations for beverages (2106.90.99) by description. The Brazil list (note 50(a)(ii)) has the same subheadings except 2106.90.44. The country lists in note 52(j) exempt 2101.30.00 and/or 2102.20.60 for Switzerland, Malaysia, Cambodia, Guatemala, Argentina, Bangladesh, Taiwan, Indonesia, Ecuador and Jordan. No Chapter 21 line is on any of the Canada Section 338 lists (note 51(b)(1)–(3), 9903.03.12–9903.03.14), which span many chapters beyond the alcoholic beverages, dairy and motor vehicles they are named for. On the China side, List 3 (note 20(f)) covers 2103.10.00, 2103.90.80 and 2106.10.00, List 4A (note 20(s)(i)) the other Chapter 21 subheadings, and no China product exclusion still in force (note 20(vvv)–(www)) names a Chapter 21 product.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 21: Miscellaneous Edible Preparations — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Food Preparations, Supplements & Sauces: FDA Rules, Quotas & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 21) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The FDA, USDA and TTB rules for each HTS Chapter 21 line — FSVP, prior notice, dietary supplement cGMP, labeling, quota licenses — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, other FTAs, quota entries, General Note 15, drawback and binding rulings.

tariffEngineering.intro:
Chapter 21 goods are food, so **FDA decides whether a shipment can be sold**: the foreign plant must be registered, prior notice must be filed before arrival, and the U.S. importer needs a foreign supplier verification program. Dietary supplements add their own manufacturing, labeling and new-ingredient rules; soups and sauces with meat can fall under USDA FSIS; compound alcoholic preparations can owe federal excise tax.

The ways to pay less are written into the schedule: claim **USMCA** or another **FTA**, enter quota goods **inside the quota** (or under a **General Note 15** exclusion), and recover duty through **drawback** when the goods are exported. Each lever depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on goods from Canada or Mexico
levers.saves: The Section 301 duty — 10% of value — plus the base rate; on the sugar and dairy quota lines, Free for Mexico at any quantity and Free inside Canada's USMCA quotas (above them Canada pays the over-quota rate plus 10%)
levers.appliesTo: All 118 lines, for goods that meet the Chapter 21 rules of origin in General Note 11
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer. It need not follow a prescribed format; it can be on the invoice or another document, and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: The rules of origin bite on ingredients: instant coffee qualifies only if non-originating coffee is no more than 60% of its weight; dairy preparations may not use non-originating Chapter 4 dairy; fortified juice concentrates may not be made from heading 2009 juice. Canadian goods on the sugar and dairy quota lines are Free only inside Canada's quota; above it they are not entered free, so they pay the over-quota rate plus the 10% Section 301 duty (and sugar-containing products may need a Canadian export certificate when USTR requires one). The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: HTSUS General Note 11 (USMCA rules of origin, Chapter 21)
USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Claim another free trade agreement
levers.saves: The base rate — for example 6.4% on most food preparations, 3% on soy sauce — on goods from Australia, Bahrain, Chile, Colombia, Israel, Jordan, South Korea, Morocco, Oman, Panama, Peru, Singapore and the CAFTA-DR countries; Japan has its own rates (JP) on some lines
levers.appliesTo: Most dutiable lines; on the sugar and dairy over-quota lines only some partners are Free, others have their own quotas in Chapter 98 subchapter XXII (9822) or Chapter 99 — Colombia, for example, is Free within its sugar quota (9822.08.01) and Free at any quantity on the dairy quota lines (9918.04.60–9918.04.80)
levers.document: The origin proof each agreement requires (a certification or declaration of origin) and records to back it up.
levers.caveat: An FTA removes the base rate but not the 2026 Section 301 duty for the 60 economies, which applies even when a special rate is claimed (U.S. note 52(a)); most of these partners are in the 60. GSP (A, A*, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Enter sugar and dairy goods inside the tariff-rate quota
levers.saves: The gap between the in-quota and over-quota rate: ice cream 20% instead of 50.2¢/kg + 17%; sweetened coffee and tea preparations 10% instead of 30.5¢/kg + 8.5%; dairy food preparations 10% instead of up to 70.4¢/kg + 8.5%; butter substitutes 15.4¢/kg instead of $1.996/kg
levers.appliesTo: The paired in-quota and over-quota lines in 2101.12, 2101.20, 2103.90, 2105.00 and 2106.90
levers.document: Butter substitutes over 45% butterfat (2106.90.24, 2106.90.34) need a USDA dairy import license (Chapter 4 additional U.S. note 14; 7 CFR part 6). The other quotas are filled at CBP in order of entry; check the quota status before shipping.
levers.caveat: Several quotas are tiny or zero: articles over 65% sugar and blended syrups have a quota of none (Chapter 17 notes 7 and 9); the 64,709-tonne quota for articles over 10% sugar runs from October 1 (note 8); mixed condiments 689 t (Chapter 21 note 4); ice cream 5,667,846 liters a year (note 5). Mexico is outside these quotas because its goods are Free under USMCA. Low-priced over-quota goods can also owe a special safeguard duty (Chapter 99 subchapter IV).

levers.title: Use a General Note 15 entry for samples, government or personal-use goods
levers.saves: The over-quota rate: these entries use the "described in general note 15" lines at the in-quota rate and are not counted against the quota
levers.document: Proof of the qualifying purpose: goods for a U.S. government agency; personal-use shipments of 5 kg or less; or samples, trade-fair, research or embassy goods that will not enter U.S. commerce, with written USDA approval presented at entry.
levers.caveat: Commercial goods do not qualify. Ask USDA for approval (identifying the product, quantity and use) before the goods ship.

levers.title: Recover duty on goods you export
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid, when the imported goods (or goods made from them) are exported or destroyed
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import and export records.
levers.caveat: Claims have filing deadlines and record-keeping rules; check with CBP whether a given Chapter 99 duty is eligible before relying on it.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty: a ruling fixes the classification — supplement (2106.90.99, 6.4%) versus medicament (3004), quota line versus non-quota line, which 2009 juice sets the rate of a fortified concentrate — before the goods arrive
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the formula or packaging decides the rate
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the product, its ingredients and packaging.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a reformulated product may need a new one.

rules.title: Food facility registration for the foreign plant that makes, packs or holds the food
Prior notice of imported food, filed before the shipment arrives
Foreign Supplier Verification Program (FSVP) kept by the U.S. importer; modified requirements for dietary supplements (21 CFR 1.511)
Food labeling: English label, ingredient list, Nutrition Facts, major allergens
Food and color additives must be approved for the use (or GRAS); colors from the listed color additives
Current good manufacturing practice and preventive controls at the foreign food plant
Shelf-stable canned or jarred soups and sauces (low-acid or acidified): plant registration and process filing
Dietary supplements: supplement cGMP, Supplement Facts label, notification for new dietary ingredients
Soups, broths and sauces containing meat or poultry may be FSIS products: eligible country and plant, reinspection at entry
In-quota butter substitutes over 45% butterfat need a dairy import license
Tariff-rate quota: in-quota rate only while the quota is open; over-quota rate afterwards
Compound alcoholic preparations (2106.90.12–2106.90.18) may owe federal excise tax on distilled spirits

groups.label: Coffee, tea & maté extracts and preparations; chicory
groups.note: The sweetened and dairy coffee and tea preparations (2101.12.32–.58, 2101.20.32–.58) sit in the sugar quotas of Chapter 17; plain extracts and instant coffee have no quota.

groups.label: Yeasts, dead single-cell micro-organisms & baking powder
Sauces, condiments, seasonings & mustard
groups.note: Shelf-stable sauces in cans or jars may be low-acid or acidified foods. Sauces with meat can be FSIS products. Seasonings with over 10% cane or beet sugar are under the 689-tonne quota (Chapter 21 note 4).

groups.label: Soups, broths & homogenized composite food (baby food)
groups.note: Soups and broths that contain meat or poultry may be USDA FSIS products rather than FDA foods; canned soups need FDA process filing.

groups.label: Ice cream & other edible ice
groups.note: Ice cream and other dairy frozen desserts are quota products (Chapter 21 note 5; Chapter 4 note 10).

groups.label: Food preparations n.e.s.i. (supplements, syrups, mixes)
groups.note: Dietary supplements (usually 2106.90.99) follow the supplement cGMP and labeling rules. Fortified juice concentrates (2106.90.52, 2106.90.54) pay the rate of the same juice in heading 2009, per liter of reconstituted juice (additional U.S. notes 1–2). In-quota butter substitutes need a USDA license; compound alcoholic preparations may owe excise tax.

tariffEngineering.disclaimer: A checklist of where the rules are, with links to the regulations — not legal advice. FDA and USDA requirements depend on the product's ingredients and form; check the agency before each new product, and CBP for quota status before each over-quota-sensitive shipment.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing Chapter 21 goods into the U.S. — HS codes, tariffs by country and quota rules. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Most Chapter 21 trade is on one line, 2106.90.99 (dietary supplements and other food preparations), at a 6.4% base rate.

The 2025 IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026. Since July 24, 2026 the extra duty is a Section 301 tariff: 10% in total for the EU, +10% or +12.5% for most other large suppliers, +20% for China (+37.5% on soy sauce and protein concentrates) and +37.5% for Brazil. USMCA-qualifying goods pay nothing extra, and instant coffee, coffee and tea extracts and fortified orange juice are exempt for everyone.
Sugar- and dairy-containing preparations, ice cream and butter substitutes are under tariff-rate quotas; above the quota the rate jumps to as much as $1.996/kg.
FDA rules decide whether the food can be sold: facility registration, prior notice, FSVP and labeling — plus cGMP and Supplement Facts for dietary supplements.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for dietary supplements?
searchedAs: harmonized tariff code for dietary supplements
faqs.answer: Most dietary supplements — tablets, capsules and powders sold as food — are food preparations of heading 2106, U.S. line 2106.90.99, with a 6.4% general rate. Products put up as medicines (measured doses for treating or preventing a disease) belong in heading 3004 instead, and supplements with over 10% milk solids or a lot of cane or beet sugar can fall on the 2106.90 quota lines. Whatever the line, FDA treats them as dietary supplements: the maker must follow the supplement cGMP rules (21 CFR part 111) and the label needs a Supplement Facts panel (21 CFR 101.36).

faqs.question: Are dietary supplements subject to tariffs?
faqs.answer: Yes. On 2106.90.99 the base rate is 6.4%, and since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 duty applies by country: 10% in total for the EU, 12.5% in total for Japan, +10% for India and the UK, +12.5% for Singapore, Vietnam and Thailand, +20% for China (26.4% in all) and +37.5% for Brazil. USMCA-qualifying supplements from Canada and Mexico pay nothing. The 2025 IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What is HTS code 2106.90?
faqs.answer: Heading 2106 is "food preparations not elsewhere specified or included". 2106.10 covers protein concentrates and textured protein (6.4%); 2106.90 covers everything else — 57 U.S. tariff lines, from compound alcoholic preparations and butter substitutes to sugar syrups, fortified juice concentrates and the 2106.90.99 basket at 6.4%, whose statistical suffixes split out drink preparations, non-dairy creamers, herbal teas, flavored honey and frozen, sugar-containing and organic food preparations. The U.S. imported $6.19B under 2106.90 in 2025, the largest product in the chapter.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on protein powder, and what is its HS code?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on protein powder
hs code for whey protein powder
faqs.answer: Protein concentrates and textured protein are 2106.10.00 (6.4%); flavored protein blends and shakes are usually 2106.90 — 2106.90.99 at 6.4%, or the dairy quota lines (10% in quota, up to 70.4¢/kg + 8.5% over quota) if they contain over 10% milk solids. Whey itself, including whey protein concentrate, is classified in Chapter 4 or heading 3502, not here. On top comes the Section 301 duty by country; China pays more on 2106.10.00 because it is on List 3: 6.4% + 12.5% + 25% = 43.9%.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for soy sauce?
faqs.answer: Soy sauce is 2103.10.00.00, with a 3% general rate. From China it pays 40.5% in total (3% + 12.5% under the 2026 Section 301 action + 25% under List 3); from Japan it is Free under the U.S.–Japan Trade Agreement but the 12.5% Japan total applies; from the EU it pays 10%; USMCA-qualifying soy sauce from Canada or Mexico is Free.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for instant coffee, and is there a tariff on it?
searchedAs: hs code for instant coffee premix
faqs.answer: Unflavored instant coffee is 2101.11.21 and other coffee extracts 2101.11.29, both Free. Both are on the Section 301 general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b)), so there is no extra duty from any of the 60 economies — Brazil included — except China's older 7.5% List 4A duty. Instant coffee premixes with sugar or milk are 2101.12: 8.5%, or the sugar quota lines (10% in quota, 30.5¢/kg + 8.5% over quota), and those do pay the Section 301 duty.

faqs.question: What is the tariff and HS code for ice cream?
faqs.answer: Ice cream is heading 2105. It is under a tariff-rate quota of 5,667,846 liters a year: 20% inside the quota (2105.00.10), 50.2¢/kg + 17% above it (2105.00.20), plus the Section 301 duty for the country. USMCA ice cream from Mexico is Free with no limit; from Canada it is Free inside Canada's USMCA quota (10,605,000 liters in 2026, shared with cream and milk drinks) and 50.2¢/liter + 17% plus the 10% Section 301 duty above it. Edible ice with no dairy limit, such as sorbet, is 2105.00.50 at 17%.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for sauces like ketchup, tomato sauce and mayonnaise?
faqs.answer: Heading 2103. Tomato ketchup is 2103.20.20 (6%), other tomato sauces 2103.20.40 (11.6%), prepared mustard 2103.30.40 (2.8¢/kg), fish sauce 2103.90.20 (Free), and mayonnaise (2103.90.90.20), salad dressings (2103.90.90.40) and most other sauces and mixed seasonings 2103.90.90 (6.4%). Seasonings with over 10% cane or beet sugar fall on the quota lines 2103.90.72–.78.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for yeast and yeast extract?
faqs.answer: Active yeasts, including instant dry baker's yeast, are 2102.10.00 (6.4%). Inactive yeasts are 2102.20: 6.4%, Free for crude dried brewers' yeast, 3.2% for other dead micro-organisms. Nonalcoholic preparations of yeast extract (other than sauces) are 2103.90.40 (3.2%). Prepared baking powder is 2102.30.00 (Free).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for soup?
faqs.answer: Soups, broths and preparations for them — including dried soup mixes and bouillon — are 2104.10.00 (3.2%), split for statistics into dried, fish-based, organic and other. Homogenized baby food in small retail containers is 2104.20. Soups with meat or poultry can be USDA FSIS products, which must come from an eligible country and plant (9 CFR part 327).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for non-dairy creamer, drink mixes and herbal tea blends?
searchedAs: hs code for non dairy creamer
hs code for powdered drink mix
faqs.answer: They are statistical suffixes of 2106.90.99 (6.4%): non-dairy coffee whiteners .75, other cream or milk substitutes .80, preparations for making beverages .71–.73 (by sweetener), and herbal teas and infusions of mixed herbs .87. A creamer or drink mix with over 10% milk solids, or with enough cane or beet sugar, moves to the 2106.90 quota lines.

faqs.question: How is a fortified juice concentrate tariffed?
faqs.answer: Vitamin- or mineral-fortified juice imported as a concentrate is Chapter 21. Fortified orange juice is 2106.90.48 at 7.85¢ per liter of reconstituted juice, and it is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty. Other single juices (2106.90.52) and juice mixtures (2106.90.54) have no printed rate: they pay the rate of the same juice in heading 2009, per liter of reconstituted juice — so the calculator cannot price them without the matching 2009 line, and the rates-by-country table shows them as text. Non-concentrated fortified juices are classified in 2202.99.
